planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed, in a well-drained bed or large container.

directions: Blue Spires forms a narrow, upright column of needle-like foliage topped with vivid deep-blue flower spikes in spring, making it a striking accent as well as a culinary rosemary. Grow in lean, gritty soil with excellent drainage, since wet roots in winter are the most common cause of loss. Once established, water only during extended dry spells and avoid heavy nitrogen feeding, which softens growth and reduces cold hardiness. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the upright habit dense and tidy.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant on a slope, wall, or raised bed where its arching branches can spill over an edge.

directions: Named for the English plantsman Collingwood Ingram, this cultivar produces long, arching stems studded with pale lavender-blue flowers in late winter and spring, and works equally well cascading over a wall or as a loose groundcover. It prefers poor to average, sharply drained soil and resents both soggy roots and heavy shade. Harvest sprigs regularly for cooking, which also helps keep the sprawling growth in bounds. In borderline climates, site it against a warm wall to boost winter survival.

planting.note: Best grown in a container or raised bed where its trailing habit and pale flowers can be shown off.

directions: Nancy Howard is a semi-trailing rosemary prized for its unusual pale pink flowers, a rare break from the typical blue-flowered forms, set against gray-green, mildly variegated foliage. Grow in full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil, and let the soil surface dry between waterings. It tolerates light shearing for culinary harvest but blooms best if pruning is limited mostly to right after flowering. Overwinter container specimens indoors in a bright, cool spot where marginal.

planting.note: Plant in a sunny, well-drained spot such as a rock garden or herb border edge.

directions: Lime Thyme is a citrus-scented lemon thyme selection whose bright, tangy-lime aroma comes through strongly when the leaves are brushed or crushed, making it popular for teas, marinades, and citrus-forward dishes. Grow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun, and avoid rich or waterlogged ground, which encourages rot and dilutes flavor. Trim back hard after flowering to maintain compact, bushy growth and encourage fresh, aromatic new leaves. It combines well with other creeping thymes in a sunny path or container planting.

planting.note: Site in full sun with sharp drainage; good as an edible edging plant.

directions: Highland Cream is a culinary common thyme cultivar with attractive cream-margined leaves that add ornamental interest without sacrificing the classic strong thyme flavor used in cooking. It grows best in poor to average, well-drained soil and full sun, and struggles in heavy, wet clay. Shear back by about a third after flowering to prevent woodiness and to keep the variegation fresh and dense. Harvest sprigs regularly through the growing season for the best flavor and to encourage compact new growth.

planting.note: Ideal for containers, edging, or tight spaces where a dwarf culinary thyme is needed.

directions: Compactus is a naturally dwarf, dense form of common culinary thyme, forming a tight mound of small aromatic leaves without the woody sprawl of the species. Grow in lean, gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, since crowded, damp conditions promote rot in the tight center of the plant. Because of its small stature, light and frequent harvesting is preferable to hard pruning. It is well suited to pots, window boxes, and the front of an herb border.

planting.note: Confine roots to a pot or buried barrier, since mint spreads aggressively by runners.

directions: Berries and Cream is a variegated mint cultivar with cream-splashed leaves and a sweet, fruity fragrance reminiscent of mixed berries, making it a favorite for iced drinks and dessert garnishes. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in part sun, and always contain the roots since it spreads as vigorously as other mints. Pinch stem tips regularly to keep growth bushy and to delay flowering, which can reduce leaf flavor. Divide congested clumps every couple of years to maintain vigor and strong variegation.
